## R Markdown

This is an R Markdown document. Markdown is a simple formatting syntax
for authoring HTML, PDF, and MS Word documents. For more details on
using R Markdown see <http://rmarkdown.rstudio.com>.

When you click the **Knit** button a document will be generated that
includes both content as well as the output of any embedded R code
chunks within the document. You can embed an R code chunk like this:

```{r cars}
summary(cars)
```

## Including Plots

You can also embed plots, for example:

```{r pressure, echo=FALSE}
plot(pressure)
```

Note that the `echo = FALSE` parameter was added to the code chunk to
prevent printing of the R code that generated the plot.

You can learn more about using R markdown files here
<https://rmarkdown.rstudio.com/lesson-3.html>

## Background

The St Louis branch of the Federal Reserve System maintains an extensive
database of U.S. economic data that is available to the public.
Economists, business, and financial institutions rely on the Federal
Reserve Economic Data (FRED) database to guide their organizations’
behaviors.

## Objective

In module 3 we introduced the R programming language. We learned the
general R syntax and how to create user defined functions that process
strings, integers, and matrices. In module 4, we practiced using an R
package called tidyverse to perform data analysis and visualization.
Tidyverse is just one of many R packages that serve to multiply the
analytical power of the language. In this activity, we will build on the
progress of previous weeks to analyze data from the Federal Reserve
Economic Data (FRED) database. A variety of open source packages have
been developed to connect the FRED database to Application Programming
Interfaces (APIs). In particular, we will use a package called fredr
(lower case) to access FRED data in the RStudio API. Then we will use
the skills learned in class to analyze and visualize the data. There are
other tools for accessing FRED data, but RStudio is perhaps the most
powerful.

## Connecting to FRED in RStudio

There are several required steps to connect RStudio API to the FRED
database. Start early so you can work through the steps. Ask the
instructor, your teammates, or schedule office hours if you need
assistance.

1.  Install the fredr package to your RStudio library. You can do this
    in one of three ways. Option a is typically the easiest.
    a.  Search fredr in the CRAN repository If prompted, you may need to
        install dependency packages or update to a recent version of R.

    b.  If you have already installed the popular devtools package, you
        can conveniently use the command
        `devtools::install_github("sboysel/fredr”)` If prompted, you may
        need to install dependency packages or update to a recent
        version of R.

    c.  The brute force, and failsafe way to install a package to
        RStudio is to save the files to your computer, then install them
        to you library by browsing for them in RStudio. Use the default
        path for “Install to Library” option.
2.  Open the fredr package, and other required packages from your
    library. If you have not already installed tidyverse and ggplot2,
    simply follow the instructions for step 1. `library(fredr)`
    `library(tidyverse)` `library(ggplot2)`

Using the provided directions, edit the following code to connect to
FRED

```{r include = FALSE}
#Install devtools and tidyverse from CRAN if needed
install.packages("devtools", repos = "[http://cran.rstudio.com/](http://cran.rstudio.com/)")
install.packages("tidyverse", repos = "[http://cran.rstudio.com/](http://cran.rstudio.com/)")

#Open devtools package to help install fredr from github
library(devtools)

#Install fredr from github
devtools::install_github("sboysel/fredr")

5.  Request the data connection using your key.

## Search for Data

The documentation for using fredr can be found at this url:
<https://github.com/sboysel/fredr> Notice that the page is a github
repository. The contents of README.md are shown as the landing page.

We now wish to search for the series ID of relevant data sets. You may
find these online or search for them with fredr. Here we search for the
top 5 data set related to the federal funds rate.

```{r}
popular_funds_series <- fredr_series_search_text(
  search_text = "federal funds",
  order_by = "popularity",
  sort_order = "desc",
  limit = 5
)

#print the search results
string_of_results<-paste(c( popular_funds_series$id), collapse=', ' )
print(paste(c("The top series id are: ", string_of_results)))


```

Save the series_id of the #1 result as a variable for later use. We also
save the FFR data as variable for inspection

```{r}
popular_funds_series_id <- popular_funds_series$id[1]



FFR_data<- fredr(
  series_id = popular_funds_series_id, # you could manually type the series id as a string on this line
  observation_start = as.Date("2003-01-01"),
  observation_end = as.Date("2023-01-01")
)

print(FFR_data)


```

Now we want to plot our top result, which should have the series ID
"FEDFUNDS". We can exploit a trick called the pipe operator, which is
included in tidyverse.

The pipe operator, %\>% is a clean way to pass an object into a
function. Here we pass the contents of popular_funds_series_id into the
`fredr()` function, and we pass the output of `fredr()` to ggplot.

```{r}
popular_funds_series_id %>%
  fredr(
    observation_start = as.Date("2003-01-01"),
    observation_end = as.Date("2023-01-01")
  ) %>%
  ggplot(data = ., mapping = aes(x = date, y = value, color = series_id)) +
  geom_line() +
  labs(x = "Observation Date", y = "Rate", color = "Series")+
  ggtitle("Federal Funds Rate\n(Effective)") +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5))
```

## Analysis Tasks

##  You are a financial analyst at a bank that sells mortgages on the
# primary market. Your manager wants to understand how historical data can
# serve as an indicator of the federal funds rate (FFR). The FFR is one of
# several factors that drive the prime rate for home mortgages.

# 1)  Plot the FFR for the past 20 years. Update dates in template as needed (1-6).

```{r ffr_plot, echo=FALSE}
library(fredr)
library(ggplot2)

popular_funds_series_id <- "FEDFUNDS"

ffr <- fredr(
  series_id = popular_funds_series_id,
  observation_start = as.Date("2005-01-01"),
  observation_end = as.Date("2025-01-01")
)

ffr_plot <- ggplot(data = ffr, aes(x = date, y = value, color = series_id)) +
  geom_line() +
  labs(x = "Observation Date", y = "FFR", color = "Series") +
  ggtitle("Federal Funds Rate\n(Effective)") +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5))

# Display the plot
ffr_plot
```
  
  
  
# 2)  Plot the 10-year treasury bond rate for the past 20 years

```{r Treasury, echo=FALSE}
TreasuryBondData <- fredr(
  series_id = "DFII10",   
  observation_start = as.Date("2005-01-01"),
  observation_end = as.Date("2025-01-01"))
  
  Treasury_plot <-
ggplot(data = TreasuryBondData, aes(x = date, y = value, color = "10-Year Bond Yield")) +
  geom_line() +
  labs(
    x = "Observation Date",
    y = "10-Year Treasury Inflation-Indexed Bond Yield (%)",
    color = "Series"
  ) +
  ggtitle("10-Year Treasury Inflation-Indexed Bond Yield (2005–2025)") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5))
  

  Treasury_plot
```

# 3)  Plot the inflation rate for the past 20 years
```{r Inflation, echo=FALSE}

  series_id = "FPCPITOTLZGUSA",   
  observation_start = as.Date("2005-01-01"),
  observation_end = as.Date("2025-01-01"))
  
Inflation_plot <-
ggplot(data = inflation_rate, aes(x = date, y = value, color = "Inflation Rate")) +

    x = "Observation Date",
    y = "Inflation rate (%)",
    color = "Series"
  ) +

  theme_minimal() +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5))


Inflation_plot
```

# 
# 5)  Provide a timeline that indicates U.S. recessions over the past 20
#  years 

```{r recessions, echo=FALSE}
recessions <- fredr(series_id = "USREC", observation_start = as.Date("2005-01-01")
,observation_end = as.Date("2025-01-01"))

Recessions_Plot <-
ggplot(recessions, aes(x = date, y = value)) +
  geom_area(fill = "grey40", alpha = 0.6) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = NULL) +  # remove y-axis labels
  labs(
    title = "U.S. Recessions (2005–2025)",
    subtitle = "Gray shaded areas indicate U.S. recession periods",
    x = "Year",
    y = NULL,
    caption = "Source: NBER via FRED (USREC)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    panel.grid = element_blank(),
    axis.ticks.y = element_blank()
  )
  


Recessions_Plot

```

```{r Money_Plot, echo=FALSE}


library(ggplot2)

recessions <- recessions %>%
  rename(Start = realtime_start , End = realtime_end)
recessions <- data.frame(
  start = as.Date(c("2007-12-01", "2020-02-01")),
  end   = as.Date(c("2009-06-01", "2020-04-01"))
)




 
My_Money_Plot <-

ggplot() +
 
  geom_rect(
    data = recessions,
    aes(xmin = start, xmax = end, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf),
    fill = "gray70", alpha = 0.5, inherit.aes = FALSE, show.legend = FALSE
  ) +
 
  geom_line(data = inflation_rate, aes(x = date, y = value, color = "Inflation Rate"), size = 1) +
  geom_line(data = ffr, aes(x = date, y = value, color = "Federal Funds Rate"), size = 1) +
  
  labs(
    title = "Money Plot: FFR, Inflation, and Recessions (2005–2025)",
    subtitle = "Gray shaded areas indicate U.S. recession periods",
    x = "Year",
    y = "Percent",
    color = NULL  # <-- This change removes the legend title
  ) +
  
  scale_color_manual(values = c("Federal Funds Rate" = "blue", "Inflation Rate" = "red")) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    legend.position = "bottom"
  )
  


My_Money_Plot

# For the money plot, I chose to combine FFR, the inflation rate, and the U.S recession periods. I chose these variables because they illustrate the relationship between both monetary policy and macroeconomic conditions. In the graph, we see that the FFR is high during periods of high inflation, but when recessions occur, there is a sharp drop-off to stimulate growth. This impacts the mortgage market because high FFRs usually lead to high mortgage rates, which reduces housing affordability and slows borrowing activity. My prediction is that the FED will slowly lower the FFR in the next year. This could lead to a slight decline in mortgage rates; however, if inflation rebounds, the FED may keep rates elevated, and this can affect mortgage affordability.#
